heart.title: Heart Anatomy
heart.intro: The heart is a fist-sized muscular pump in the middle of the chest, tilted so that two-thirds of it lies to the left of the midline. Its four chambers and four valves move about five litres of blood every minute at rest, sending deoxygenated blood to the lungs and oxygenated blood to the rest of the body.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Middle mediastinum, behind the sternum, between the lungs, resting on the diaphragm

keyFacts.label: Chambers
keyFacts.value: Right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle

keyFacts.label: Valves
keyFacts.value: Tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral, aortic

keyFacts.label: Weight
keyFacts.value: About 250-350 g in adults

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Right and left coronary arteries from the ascending aorta

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Sympathetic fibres (speed up) and the vagus nerve (slow down) via the cardiac plexus

keyFacts.label: Output
keyFacts.value: About 5 L/min at rest, up to 25 L/min in exercise

sections.heading: Location and coverings
sections.body: The heart sits in the middle mediastinum, enclosed in the pericardium: a tough fibrous outer sac fused to the diaphragm below and the great vessels above, lined by a double layer of serous membrane whose thin film of fluid lets the heart beat almost without friction. The apex points down and to the left, reaching the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, where the apex beat can be felt. The base faces backwards, towards the oesophagus and descending aorta, which is why an oesophageal ultrasound probe gives such clear views of the atria.

sections.heading: Chambers
sections.body: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus, and passes it through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, a thin-walled crescent-shaped chamber that pumps into the pulmonary trunk. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood through four pulmonary veins and fills the left ventricle, whose wall is about three times thicker than the right because it must generate pressures of 120 mmHg or more to drive blood around the whole body. The interatrial and interventricular septa separate the two sides; the foramen ovale, open before birth, leaves a small depression in the interatrial septum.

sections.heading: Valves
sections.body: Two atrioventricular valves (the tricuspid on the right and the mitral, with two leaflets, on the left) are held closed during ventricular contraction by chordae tendineae anchored to papillary muscles, so they cannot balloon back into the atria. Two semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic), each with three cusps, prevent blood ejected from the ventricles from flowing back. The valve rings sit in a fibrous skeleton that also insulates the atria electrically from the ventricles, so that the only electrical route between them is the atrioventricular node and bundle.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: The right and left coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve and fill mainly during diastole. The left coronary artery divides within a few centimetres into the anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery, running down the front of the interventricular septum, and the circumflex artery, curving round in the left atrioventricular groove. The right coronary artery runs in the right atrioventricular groove, usually giving off the sinoatrial nodal artery and, in most people, the posterior interventricular artery that supplies the inferior wall. Blockage of any of these branches starves a predictable territory of muscle.

sections.heading: Venous drainage
sections.body: Most venous blood from the heart wall collects in the coronary sinus, a wide vein in the posterior atrioventricular groove that empties into the right atrium; the great, middle and small cardiac veins are its main tributaries. Small anterior cardiac veins and the tiny thebesian veins drain directly into the chambers.

sections.heading: Innervation and conduction
sections.body: The heart beats on its own: the sinoatrial node in the right atrial wall near the superior vena cava fires about 70 times a minute, the impulse spreads across the atria to the atrioventricular node, pauses, then races down the bundle of His and its branches to the ventricular muscle. The autonomic nervous system only modulates this rhythm. Sympathetic fibres from the upper thoracic spinal cord increase rate and force; parasympathetic fibres in the vagus nerve slow it. Pain from the heart is referred to the chest, left arm, neck and jaw because those areas share spinal cord segments with the cardiac sympathetic nerves.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: Each cardiac cycle has a filling phase (diastole) and a contraction phase (systole). The right side of the heart sends blood through the pulmonary circulation to pick up oxygen and unload carbon dioxide; the left side sends it through the systemic circulation. Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume, and both are adjusted continuously by nerves, hormones and the volume of blood returning to the heart.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Narrowing of the coronary arteries causes angina and heart attacks; the territory affected shows on the ECG and echocardiogram. Valve disease (a leaking mitral valve, a narrowed aortic valve) can be heard as murmurs and measured with ultrasound. Failure of the pump causes fluid to back up into the lungs and legs. Disorders of the conduction system cause slow, fast or irregular rhythms such as atrial fibrillation. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation works because the heart lies directly behind the lower sternum, where compressions squeeze it against the spine.

brain.title: Brain Anatomy
brain.descriptor: Lobes, Deep Structures, Blood Supply & Function
brain.intro: The brain is about 1.4 kg of nervous tissue floating in cerebrospinal fluid inside the skull. Its wrinkled cerebral hemispheres handle perception, movement, language, memory and planning; the cerebellum coordinates movement; and the brainstem keeps breathing, heart rate and consciousness going.

keyFacts.label: Weight
keyFacts.value: About 1.3-1.4 kg, 2% of body weight, using 20% of the body's oxygen

keyFacts.label: Main parts
keyFacts.value: Cerebrum (two hemispheres), diencephalon (thalamus, hypothalamus), brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla), cerebellum

keyFacts.label: Lobes
keyFacts.value: Frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, plus the insula and limbic lobe

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Two internal carotid and two vertebral arteries joining at the circle of Willis

keyFacts.label: Protection
keyFacts.value: Skull, three meninges and about 150 mL of cerebrospinal fluid

keyFacts.label: Neurons
keyFacts.value: Roughly 86 billion

sections.heading: Location and coverings
sections.body: The brain fills the cranial cavity and is wrapped in three meninges: the tough dura mater lining the skull, the spidery arachnoid, and the delicate pia mater clinging to every fold. Cerebrospinal fluid made in the ventricles circulates in the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia, cushioning the brain and reducing its effective weight to a few tens of grams. The brain leaves the skull through the foramen magnum as the spinal cord.

sections.heading: Cerebral hemispheres and lobes
sections.body: Each hemisphere is folded into gyri separated by sulci, which triples the surface area of the cortex. The central sulcus divides the frontal lobe (movement, planning, speech production in Broca's area, personality) from the parietal lobe (touch, spatial awareness); the lateral sulcus marks off the temporal lobe (hearing, language comprehension in Wernicke's area, memory via the hippocampus); the occipital lobe at the back is vision. The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex and the postcentral gyrus the primary somatosensory cortex, each mapping the opposite side of the body. The corpus callosum, a thick band of white matter, connects the two hemispheres.

sections.heading: Deep structures
sections.body: Beneath the cortex lie the basal ganglia (caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus), which shape movement and are lost in Parkinson's disease; the thalamus, the relay station for almost all sensation on its way to the cortex; and the hypothalamus, which controls hunger, thirst, temperature, sleep and the pituitary gland below it. The hippocampus and amygdala in the medial temporal lobe form new memories and process emotion.

sections.heading: Brainstem and cerebellum
sections.body: The midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata carry every tract between the brain and spinal cord and house the nuclei of ten of the twelve cranial nerves, the breathing and cardiovascular centres, and the reticular formation that maintains wakefulness. The cerebellum, tucked beneath the occipital lobes, compares intended with actual movement and corrects it, giving smooth, coordinated action and balance.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: The internal carotid arteries supply the front two-thirds of each hemisphere through the anterior and middle cerebral arteries; the vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery, which supplies the brainstem, cerebellum and, through the posterior cerebral arteries, the occipital lobes. These vessels meet at the circle of Willis on the underside of the brain, a ring that can partly compensate for a blocked artery. The middle cerebral artery is the vessel most often blocked in stroke; because it supplies the motor and language areas, its blockage causes the face, arm and speech signs of the FAST test.

sections.heading: Venous drainage
sections.body: Cerebral veins drain into the dural venous sinuses, channels between the layers of dura: the superior sagittal sinus along the top of the brain, the transverse and sigmoid sinuses curving down to become the internal jugular veins. Cerebrospinal fluid is absorbed into the same sinuses through arachnoid granulations.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: Sensory information from the body crosses to the opposite hemisphere, so the left brain controls and feels the right side of the body. Language is usually left-hemisphere dominant. Neurons communicate with electrical impulses and chemical neurotransmitters; the pattern of connections, refined throughout life, underlies learning and memory.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Stroke, tumours, trauma, infection and degenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's each damage particular regions, and the resulting deficits map back onto the anatomy: weakness from the motor cortex or internal capsule, memory loss from the hippocampus, tremor and rigidity from the basal ganglia, unsteadiness from the cerebellum. Raised pressure inside the rigid skull, from bleeding or swelling, is dangerous because the brain can be pushed through the openings in the dura and the foramen magnum.

structures: Sphenoid part of left middle cerebral artery

lungs.title: Lung Anatomy
lungs.descriptor: Lobes, Airways, Blood Supply & Gas Exchange
lungs.intro: The lungs are two spongy, cone-shaped organs filling most of the chest on either side of the heart. Air reaches them through a branching tree of airways ending in about 300 million alveoli, whose combined surface, roughly the size of a tennis court, is where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it.

keyFacts.label: Lobes
keyFacts.value: Three on the right (upper, middle, lower), two on the left (upper, lower) with a lingula

keyFacts.label: Airways
keyFacts.value: Trachea, main bronchi, lobar and segmental bronchi, bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli

keyFacts.label: Segments
keyFacts.value: 10 bronchopulmonary segments per lung, each with its own bronchus and artery

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Pulmonary arteries (for gas exchange) and bronchial arteries (for the lung tissue itself)

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Vagus nerve (constricts airways, mucus) and sympathetic fibres (dilate airways)

keyFacts.label: Breathing
keyFacts.value: About 12-16 breaths a minute at rest, 500 mL each

sections.heading: Location and pleura
sections.body: Each lung sits in its own pleural cavity, wrapped in visceral pleura that is continuous with the parietal pleura lining the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum. The thin film of fluid between the two layers lets the lung slide as the chest expands and holds it against the chest wall by surface tension, so that when the diaphragm descends the lung is pulled open. Air entering this space (a pneumothorax) breaks the seal and the lung collapses. The right lung is larger and shorter, pushed up by the liver; the left has a cardiac notch that makes room for the heart.

sections.heading: Lobes and segments
sections.body: Fissures divide the right lung into upper, middle and lower lobes and the left into upper and lower lobes. Each lobe is built from bronchopulmonary segments, pyramids of lung tissue with their own segmental bronchus and artery and no connection to their neighbours, which is why surgeons can remove one segment and radiologists describe a shadow by segment.

sections.heading: Airways
sections.body: The trachea divides at the carina into right and left main bronchi. The right is wider and more vertical, so inhaled objects usually go that way. Each main bronchus divides into lobar, then segmental bronchi, then some twenty further generations of ever-smaller bronchi and bronchioles. Cartilage rings stiffen the larger airways; smooth muscle in the bronchioles adjusts their calibre, tightening in asthma. Ciliated cells and mucus sweep dust and microbes upward to be swallowed. Beyond the terminal bronchioles, respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts open into clusters of alveoli.

sections.heading: Alveoli and gas exchange
sections.body: An alveolus is a thin-walled sac about 0.2 mm across, lined by flat type I cells for gas exchange and type II cells that secrete surfactant, the detergent that stops the sacs collapsing at the end of each breath. Capillaries form a dense net around every alveolus, so the barrier between air and blood is under a micrometre thick. Oxygen diffuses into red cells and binds haemoglobin; carbon dioxide diffuses the other way and is breathed out.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: The pulmonary trunk from the right ventricle divides into right and left pulmonary arteries, which follow the bronchi into every segment and carry deoxygenated blood to the alveolar capillaries. Four pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium. Separately, small bronchial arteries from the aorta nourish the bronchi and lung tissue. A clot lodging in a pulmonary artery (pulmonary embolism) blocks flow to the segment it serves.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: The pulmonary plexus around each lung root carries parasympathetic fibres from the vagus nerve, which constrict the airways and stimulate mucus, and sympathetic fibres, which relax airway muscle. Salbutamol and adrenaline relieve wheeze by acting on the same beta-2 receptors that the sympathetic nerves use. The lung itself has no pain fibres; chest pain from lung disease comes from the parietal pleura, supplied by the intercostal and phrenic nerves.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: Breathing in is active: the diaphragm flattens and the external intercostals lift the ribs, enlarging the chest so air flows in. Breathing out at rest is passive elastic recoil. The brainstem sets the rhythm, driven mainly by the level of carbon dioxide in the blood. Beyond gas exchange the lungs filter small clots, make angiotensin-converting enzyme, and defend against inhaled microbes.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Asthma and COPD narrow the airways; pneumonia fills alveoli with fluid and pus; fibrosis stiffens the lung; emphysema destroys alveolar walls; cancer most often arises from the bronchial lining. Spirometry measures how much and how fast air moves; a chest X-ray and CT show the lobes, segments and pleural spaces; a pulse oximeter reads how well the alveoli are loading oxygen onto haemoglobin.

liver.title: Liver Anatomy
liver.intro: The liver is the largest internal organ, about 1.5 kg of chemical factory tucked under the right ribs. It receives nutrient-rich blood from the gut through the portal vein, processes and stores what the body needs, neutralises toxins, makes bile and most of the proteins in the blood, and can regenerate after losing more than half its mass.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Right upper abdomen under the diaphragm, protected by ribs 7-11

keyFacts.label: Weight
keyFacts.value: About 1.4-1.6 kg

keyFacts.label: Lobes
keyFacts.value: Right and left (with the small caudate and quadrate lobes); eight functional Couinaud segments

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Hepatic portal vein (75%) and hepatic artery (25%), about 1.5 L/min

keyFacts.label: Drainage
keyFacts.value: Hepatic veins to the inferior vena cava; bile through the hepatic ducts

keyFacts.label: Cells
keyFacts.value: Hepatocytes arranged in plates around sinusoids; Kupffer cells filter the blood

sections.heading: Location and surfaces
sections.body: The liver lies against the underside of the diaphragm, mostly behind the right lower ribs, its left lobe reaching across to the stomach. Its smooth diaphragmatic surface is covered by peritoneum except for a bare area against the diaphragm; its visceral surface is moulded by the gallbladder, duodenum, right kidney and colon. The falciform ligament attaches it to the front abdominal wall and marks the boundary between the anatomical right and left lobes.

sections.heading: Lobes and segments
sections.body: For surgery the liver is divided into eight Couinaud segments, each with its own branch of the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, separated by planes that contain the hepatic veins. Segments II-IV form the functional left liver and V-VIII the right; segment I is the caudate lobe, which drains straight into the vena cava. A surgeon can remove any segment or group of segments along these planes with little bleeding and no loss of function in the remainder.

sections.heading: The porta hepatis and bile ducts
sections.body: The portal vein, hepatic artery and common hepatic duct enter and leave the liver at the porta hepatis on its underside, wrapped together in the hepatoduodenal ligament. Bile made by hepatocytes flows through tiny canaliculi into ductules and then the right and left hepatic ducts, which join as the common hepatic duct; the cystic duct from the gallbladder joins it to form the common bile duct, which opens into the duodenum beside the pancreatic duct.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: Uniquely, most of the liver's blood is venous: the hepatic portal vein brings blood that has already passed through the stomach, intestines, pancreas and spleen, loaded with absorbed nutrients, gut hormones and anything else taken by mouth, including drugs and toxins. The hepatic artery, a branch of the coeliac trunk, brings oxygenated blood. Both mix in the sinusoids between plates of hepatocytes. Because everything absorbed from the gut passes through the liver first, oral drugs can be partly destroyed before reaching the circulation (the first-pass effect).

sections.heading: Venous drainage
sections.body: Blood leaves through three hepatic veins that open into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm. When the liver is scarred by cirrhosis, resistance rises, pressure backs up in the portal system, and blood finds alternative routes through veins around the oesophagus and stomach, which can bleed catastrophically.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Sympathetic fibres from the coeliac plexus and parasympathetic fibres from the vagus reach the liver along its vessels. The liver's own tissue is insensitive to pain; the ache of a swollen liver comes from stretch of its capsule and the overlying peritoneum, and is often felt at the right shoulder because the phrenic nerve shares spinal segments with the shoulder skin.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The liver stores glucose as glycogen and releases it between meals, makes new glucose from amino acids, builds plasma proteins including albumin and the clotting factors, manufactures cholesterol and bile salts, stores iron and vitamins A, D and B12, breaks down worn-out red cells into bilirubin, converts ammonia to urea, and inactivates hormones, alcohol and most drugs through its cytochrome enzymes.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Fatty liver, alcohol and viral hepatitis inflame and eventually scar the liver; cirrhosis blocks portal flow and cripples synthesis, so patients bleed, swell with ascites and become jaundiced and confused. Liver function tests read these processes in the blood. Gallstones can block the common bile duct, causing jaundice and pancreatitis. The liver is the commonest site for cancer to spread through the portal vein from the bowel. Paracetamol overdose destroys hepatocytes within days.

kidneys.title: Kidney Anatomy
kidneys.intro: The two kidneys are bean-shaped organs the size of a fist, lying against the back wall of the abdomen on either side of the spine. Each contains about a million nephrons that filter the entire blood volume some sixty times a day, keeping water, salts and acid in balance and clearing waste into the urine.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Retroperitoneal, T12-L3, the right kidney slightly lower because of the liver

keyFacts.label: Size
keyFacts.value: About 11 cm long, 150 g each

keyFacts.label: Working units
keyFacts.value: About one million nephrons per kidney

keyFacts.label: Blood flow
keyFacts.value: Around 1.2 L/min, a fifth of cardiac output

keyFacts.label: Filtration
keyFacts.value: About 180 L of filtrate a day, 99% reabsorbed

keyFacts.label: Hormones
keyFacts.value: Renin, erythropoietin, active vitamin D

sections.heading: Location and coverings
sections.body: The kidneys lie behind the peritoneum against the psoas and quadratus lumborum muscles, the upper poles tucked under the eleventh and twelfth ribs, with the adrenal gland capping each. A tough fibrous capsule, a layer of perirenal fat and the renal fascia hold them in place and cushion them. Because they sit so far back, kidney pain is felt in the loin and can be tested by tapping the renal angle between the last rib and the spine.

sections.heading: Internal structure
sections.body: A cut kidney shows an outer cortex and inner medulla arranged as renal pyramids, whose tips (papillae) drip urine into cup-shaped minor calyces. These join into major calyces and then the renal pelvis, the funnel that narrows into the ureter at the hilum, where the renal artery enters and the renal vein leaves. Stones formed in the calyces cause agonising pain as they pass into the ureter.

sections.heading: The nephron
sections.body: Each nephron begins with a glomerulus, a tuft of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule, where blood pressure forces water and small solutes through a filter that holds back cells and proteins. The filtrate then passes along the proximal tubule (bulk reabsorption of water, glucose, salts), the loop of Henle dipping into the medulla (creating the salt gradient that lets urine be concentrated), the distal tubule and the collecting duct, where hormones fine-tune how much water and salt is returned to the blood. Diuretics such as furosemide act on the loop; ACE inhibitors lower the pressure in the glomerulus.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: Each renal artery arises directly from the abdominal aorta and divides into segmental, interlobar, arcuate and interlobular arteries before feeding the glomeruli through afferent arterioles. Blood leaves the glomerulus by an efferent arteriole into a second capillary network around the tubules, then into the renal vein and inferior vena cava. Narrowing of a renal artery drives up blood pressure through renin release.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Sympathetic nerves from the renal plexus constrict the renal vessels and stimulate renin; there is little parasympathetic supply. Pain from a stone is carried with the sympathetic fibres to spinal segments T11-L2 and referred along the loin, groin and, in men, the testis.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The kidneys hold the composition of the blood steady: they excrete urea, creatinine and drugs, regulate sodium, potassium, calcium and phosphate, correct acid-base balance by excreting acid and regenerating bicarbonate, and adjust water excretion under antidiuretic hormone so that blood concentration stays within one or two per cent. They release renin to control blood pressure, erythropoietin to drive red cell production, and activate vitamin D for the bones.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Diabetes and high blood pressure slowly damage the glomeruli, leaking protein into the urine and lowering the filtration rate: chronic kidney disease. Sudden injury from dehydration, sepsis or drugs shows as a rising creatinine. Stones, infection and obstruction affect the collecting system. When function falls below about a tenth, dialysis or a transplant replaces the filtering.

references.title: NIH NIDDK: Your kidneys and how they work

stomach.title: Stomach Anatomy
stomach.intro: The stomach is a muscular, J-shaped bag in the upper left abdomen that receives food from the oesophagus, churns it with acid and enzymes into a paste called chyme, and releases it in small amounts into the duodenum. Its lining secretes about two litres of gastric juice a day and protects itself with a layer of mucus and bicarbonate.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Left upper abdomen under the diaphragm, between the oesophagus and duodenum

keyFacts.label: Regions
keyFacts.value: Cardia, fundus, body, antrum, pylorus

keyFacts.label: Capacity
keyFacts.value: About 50 mL empty, 1-1.5 L after a meal, up to 4 L

keyFacts.label: Secretions
keyFacts.value: Hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen, intrinsic factor, mucus, gastrin, ghrelin

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Branches of the coeliac trunk: left and right gastric, gastro-epiploic and short gastric arteries

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Vagus nerves (secretion, motility) and sympathetic fibres from the coeliac plexus

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The stomach lies in the left hypochondrium and epigastrium, below the diaphragm and the left lobe of the liver, in front of the pancreas, spleen and left kidney. Its lesser curvature faces the liver and its greater curvature carries the apron-like greater omentum. The lower oesophageal sphincter at the cardia stops acid refluxing upward; the pyloric sphincter at the outlet controls emptying into the duodenum.

sections.heading: Regions
sections.body: The cardia surrounds the oesophageal opening; the fundus is the dome that rises above it, often full of swallowed air; the body is the main reservoir; the antrum grinds food against the closed pylorus and releases the hormone gastrin; and the pylorus is the thick muscular outlet. Ulcers favour the lesser curvature and the antrum; the fundus and body carry the acid-secreting glands.

sections.heading: Wall and lining
sections.body: Three layers of smooth muscle (an extra oblique layer inside the usual circular and longitudinal coats) let the stomach churn as well as squeeze. The mucosa is thrown into folds (rugae) that flatten as it fills and is packed with gastric pits leading to glands: parietal cells make hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor (needed to absorb vitamin B12), chief cells make pepsinogen, and mucous cells coat the surface with alkaline mucus. Proton pump inhibitors shut down the acid pump in the parietal cells.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: All of the stomach's arteries come from the coeliac trunk: the left gastric runs along the lesser curvature to meet the right gastric from the hepatic artery, the right and left gastro-epiploic arteries run along the greater curvature, and short gastric arteries from the splenic artery reach the fundus. This rich supply is why bleeding ulcers can be life-threatening, and why the stomach can be reshaped in surgery without losing its blood supply.

sections.heading: Venous drainage
sections.body: Gastric veins accompany the arteries and drain into the portal vein, so stomach blood reaches the liver first. In cirrhosis, veins around the cardia enlarge into varices that can rupture.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: The anterior and posterior vagal trunks enter the abdomen on the oesophagus and supply the stomach: they trigger acid secretion in anticipation of food and drive the peristaltic waves that mix and empty it. Sympathetic fibres reduce motility and carry pain, which is felt in the epigastrium.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The stomach stores a meal, kills most swallowed microbes with acid at pH 1-2, begins protein digestion with pepsin, mixes everything into chyme and meters it into the duodenum at a rate the small intestine can handle, roughly 2-4 hours for a mixed meal. It signals hunger with ghrelin and fullness through stretch receptors.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Acid reflux irritates the oesophagus when the lower sphincter fails; Helicobacter pylori infection and anti-inflammatory drugs breach the mucus barrier and cause gastritis and peptic ulcers; stomach cancer arises from the lining. A gastroscopy passes a camera through the cardia to inspect every region and take biopsies.

references.title: NIH NIDDK: Your digestive system and how it works

pancreas.title: Pancreas Anatomy
pancreas.intro: The pancreas is a soft, elongated gland about 15 cm long lying across the back of the upper abdomen behind the stomach. It is two organs in one: exocrine tissue that pours digestive enzymes into the duodenum, and scattered islets that release insulin and glucagon into the blood to control glucose.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Retroperitoneal, across L1-L2, head in the curve of the duodenum, tail reaching the spleen

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Head (with uncinate process), neck, body, tail

keyFacts.label: Ducts
keyFacts.value: Main pancreatic duct joining the common bile duct at the ampulla; accessory duct

keyFacts.label: Exocrine output
keyFacts.value: About 1.5 L of alkaline enzyme-rich juice a day

keyFacts.label: Endocrine cells
keyFacts.value: About a million islets of Langerhans: beta cells (insulin), alpha cells (glucagon), delta cells (somatostatin)

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Pancreaticoduodenal arteries and branches of the splenic artery

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The pancreas lies behind the peritoneum of the lesser sac, with the stomach in front of it and the aorta, inferior vena cava, left kidney and spine behind. Its head nestles in the C-shaped curve of the duodenum, the neck lies over the superior mesenteric vessels, and the tail reaches the hilum of the spleen. Being so deep, the pancreas is hard to examine and its disease often presents late; its pain radiates through to the back.

sections.heading: Ducts
sections.body: The main pancreatic duct runs the length of the gland collecting from lobular ducts and, in most people, joins the common bile duct to open into the duodenum at the major papilla, guarded by the sphincter of Oddi. A gallstone lodging here blocks both ducts, causing jaundice and pancreatitis. The smaller accessory duct opens separately a little higher.

sections.heading: Exocrine tissue
sections.body: Acinar cells make inactive enzyme precursors (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, lipase, amylase) and duct cells add bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralises stomach acid. The enzymes are only activated in the duodenum, a safeguard that fails in pancreatitis, when the gland digests itself.

sections.heading: Islets
sections.body: Islets of Langerhans, more numerous in the tail, sense blood glucose directly. Beta cells release insulin after meals so that muscle, fat and liver take up glucose; alpha cells release glucagon between meals to mobilise it. Autoimmune destruction of beta cells causes type 1 diabetes; resistance to insulin with failing beta-cell reserve causes type 2.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: The head is supplied by the superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries from the gastroduodenal artery and the inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries from the superior mesenteric artery, which form arcades shared with the duodenum, so the two cannot be separated in surgery (the Whipple operation removes both). The body and tail receive branches from the splenic artery as it runs along the upper border. Veins drain to the splenic and superior mesenteric veins and thus the portal vein.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Vagal fibres stimulate secretion; sympathetic fibres from the coeliac and superior mesenteric plexuses carry pain to T6-T10, which is why pancreatic pain bores through to the mid-back. Coeliac plexus block is used to relieve pain in pancreatic cancer.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Acute pancreatitis, usually from gallstones or alcohol, causes severe upper abdominal pain and a raised blood lipase or amylase. Chronic pancreatitis destroys both functions, causing diabetes and fatty stools. Pancreatic cancer in the head presents with painless jaundice from bile duct obstruction. Blood glucose and HbA1c measure the islets' work.

aorta.title: Aorta Anatomy
aorta.intro: The aorta is the largest artery in the body, a thick elastic tube about 2.5-3 cm wide that carries every drop of oxygenated blood from the left ventricle. It rises from the heart, arches over it, and descends through the chest and abdomen, giving branches to every organ before dividing into the two common iliac arteries.

keyFacts.label: Segments
keyFacts.value: Ascending aorta, arch, descending thoracic aorta, abdominal aorta

keyFacts.label: Length
keyFacts.value: About 30-40 cm; ends at L4 by dividing into the common iliac arteries

keyFacts.label: Arch branches
keyFacts.value: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian

keyFacts.label: Abdominal branches
keyFacts.value: Coeliac trunk, superior mesenteric, renal, gonadal and inferior mesenteric arteries

keyFacts.label: Wall
keyFacts.value: Three layers rich in elastin that store energy in systole and keep blood flowing in diastole

keyFacts.label: Pressure
keyFacts.value: About 120/80 mmHg at rest

sections.heading: Ascending aorta
sections.body: The aorta begins at the aortic valve inside the pericardium. Its first centimetres bulge into three aortic sinuses, from two of which the right and left coronary arteries arise, so the heart muscle is the first tissue the aorta supplies. The ascending aorta runs up and to the right for about 5 cm before curving into the arch.

sections.heading: Arch
sections.body: The arch passes backwards and to the left over the left main bronchus and the pulmonary trunk, at the level of the sternal angle, giving off three great branches from its upper surface: the brachiocephalic trunk (which divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries), the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery. Baroreceptors in the arch report blood pressure to the brainstem; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under it, so an enlarged arch can cause hoarseness.

sections.heading: Descending thoracic aorta
sections.body: From the arch the aorta descends on the left side of the spine, then behind the oesophagus, to pass through the diaphragm at T12. It gives posterior intercostal arteries to the chest wall, bronchial arteries to the lungs, oesophageal branches and small vessels to the pericardium and diaphragm.

sections.heading: Abdominal aorta
sections.body: In the abdomen the aorta lies to the left of the inferior vena cava, in front of the lumbar spine. Three unpaired branches supply the gut: the coeliac trunk (stomach, liver, spleen, pancreas), the superior mesenteric artery (small intestine and right colon) and the inferior mesenteric artery (left colon and rectum). Paired branches go to the adrenals, kidneys and gonads, and lumbar arteries to the back wall. At L4, level with the top of the hip bones, it divides into the common iliac arteries, which supply the pelvis and legs.

sections.heading: Wall structure and function
sections.body: The aortic wall has an inner intima, a thick media of elastic lamellae and smooth muscle, and an outer adventitia carrying its own tiny vessels. During systole the elastic wall stretches to accept the ejected blood; during diastole it recoils and keeps blood flowing forward, smoothing the pulse. With age the elastin fragments, the aorta stiffens and systolic pressure rises.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Atherosclerosis roughens the aorta and its branches; cholesterol and blood pressure drive it. An aneurysm, most often of the abdominal aorta below the kidneys, can rupture with catastrophic bleeding, which is why men over 65 are offered a screening ultrasound. Aortic dissection, a tear in the intima that lets blood split the wall, causes tearing chest pain radiating to the back and is a surgical emergency. Coarctation is a congenital narrowing near the arch. Aortic valve stenosis obstructs the outlet from the heart.

coronary.title: Coronary Arteries Anatomy
coronary.intro: The coronary arteries are the heart's own blood supply: two vessels a few millimetres wide that arise from the aorta just above the aortic valve and run over the surface of the heart, sending branches into the muscle. Because each branch supplies a fixed territory, a blockage produces a predictable pattern of damage that the ECG, echocardiogram and angiogram can map.

keyFacts.label: Origin
keyFacts.value: Right and left aortic sinuses, just above the aortic valve

keyFacts.label: Left coronary artery
keyFacts.value: Short main stem dividing into the left anterior descending (anterior interventricular) and circumflex arteries

keyFacts.label: Right coronary artery
keyFacts.value: Runs in the right atrioventricular groove; gives the posterior interventricular artery in about 85% of people (right dominance)

keyFacts.label: Filling
keyFacts.value: Mainly during diastole, when the relaxed muscle lets blood through

keyFacts.label: Venous return
keyFacts.value: Great, middle and small cardiac veins to the coronary sinus

keyFacts.label: Flow
keyFacts.value: About 250 mL/min at rest, five times more in exercise

sections.heading: Left coronary artery
sections.body: The left main stem is only 1-2 cm long before it divides. The anterior interventricular branch, known clinically as the left anterior descending (LAD) artery, runs down the front of the interventricular groove to the apex, giving diagonal branches to the front of the left ventricle and septal branches into the septum; it supplies about half the left ventricle and most of the conduction bundles, which is why an LAD occlusion is the most dangerous heart attack. The circumflex artery curves round the left side in the atrioventricular groove, giving obtuse marginal branches to the lateral wall.

sections.heading: Right coronary artery
sections.body: The right coronary artery runs in the right atrioventricular groove, giving a branch to the sinoatrial node in most people, acute marginal branches to the right ventricle, and, in about 85% of people, the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery and a branch to the atrioventricular node. It supplies the right ventricle, the inferior wall of the left ventricle and the conduction nodes, so its blockage causes inferior infarcts often complicated by slow rhythms.

sections.heading: Dominance and variation
sections.body: The artery that gives off the posterior interventricular branch is called dominant: right in most people, left in about 8%, and shared in the rest. Anatomy varies enough that every angiogram is read individually. Collateral vessels between territories enlarge slowly when an artery narrows, which is why a chronic blockage can be survived while a sudden one is not.

sections.heading: Venous drainage
sections.body: The great cardiac vein accompanies the anterior interventricular artery and curves round with the circumflex into the coronary sinus, which runs in the posterior atrioventricular groove and empties into the right atrium; the middle cardiac vein follows the posterior interventricular artery. Pacing leads for heart failure are threaded through the coronary sinus to reach the left ventricle.

sections.heading: Physiology
sections.body: The coronary arteries are compressed by the contracting muscle, so most flow occurs in diastole. A fast heart rate shortens diastole and reduces supply just when demand rises. The vessels dilate in response to adenosine and nitric oxide released by working muscle; nitrates such as glyceryl trinitrate use the same pathway.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Fatty plaques in the wall narrow the lumen and cause angina on exertion; a ruptured plaque triggers a clot that blocks the artery and kills the muscle downstream within hours, a myocardial infarction. Troponin in the blood confirms damage, the ECG localises it, and an angiogram through a wrist or groin artery shows the blockage so that it can be opened with a balloon and stent or bypassed with a graft. Statins, aspirin and blood-pressure control slow the disease.

knee.title: Knee Joint Anatomy
knee.intro: The knee is the largest joint in the body: a hinge between the femur and tibia, with the patella gliding in front, held together by four main ligaments and cushioned by two menisci. It bears several times body weight with every step and is the joint most often injured in sport and most often replaced in later life.

keyFacts.label: Type
keyFacts.value: Modified hinge (synovial) joint: flexion, extension and a little rotation

keyFacts.label: Bones
keyFacts.value: Femoral condyles, tibial plateau, patella; the fibula lies alongside but is not part of the joint

keyFacts.label: Ligaments
keyFacts.value: Anterior and posterior cruciate, medial and lateral collateral, patellar ligament

keyFacts.label: Menisci
keyFacts.value: Medial (C-shaped) and lateral (more circular) fibrocartilage pads

keyFacts.label: Movement
keyFacts.value: About 0-140 degrees of flexion; the joint locks in full extension

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Genicular branches of the popliteal artery

sections.heading: Bones and surfaces
sections.body: The rounded femoral condyles roll and glide on the almost flat tibial plateau, an unstable arrangement that depends entirely on ligaments and muscles for stability. The patella, a sesamoid bone in the quadriceps tendon, slides in the groove between the condyles and increases the leverage of the quadriceps. The head of the fibula articulates with the tibia below the joint line and anchors the lateral collateral ligament.

sections.heading: Ligaments
sections.body: Inside the joint the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) stops the tibia sliding forward and limits rotation; the posterior cruciate stops it sliding back. The medial collateral ligament resists the knee being forced inwards (valgus) and blends with the medial meniscus; the lateral collateral is a separate cord resisting varus force. The patellar ligament carries the quadriceps pull from the patella to the tibial tuberosity. A twisting fall tears the ACL with a pop and rapid swelling; a blow to the outside of the knee sprains the medial collateral.

sections.heading: Menisci
sections.body: Two crescents of fibrocartilage deepen the tibial surface, spread the load over the cartilage and absorb shock. Their outer third has a blood supply and can heal; the inner part does not. Tears cause pain along the joint line, catching and locking, and are seen on MRI or arthroscopy.

sections.heading: Capsule, bursae and synovium
sections.body: A fibrous capsule lined with synovial membrane surrounds the joint and produces the lubricating fluid; an effusion (water on the knee) stretches it. Several bursae reduce friction, including the prepatellar bursa in front of the kneecap (housemaid's knee when inflamed) and a bursa behind the knee that can swell into a Baker's cyst.

sections.heading: Muscles and movement
sections.body: The quadriceps extend the knee and the hamstrings flex it; the gastrocnemius, popliteus and the iliotibial tract also cross the joint. In the last degrees of extension the femur rotates medially on the tibia, screwing the joint tight so that standing needs little muscular effort; the popliteus unlocks it. Strong quadriceps and hamstrings are the best protection for the ligaments.

sections.heading: Blood and nerve supply
sections.body: The popliteal artery passes behind the knee and sends genicular branches around the joint that form an anastomosis, a safety net if the main artery is compressed. The tibial and common fibular nerves pass behind and beside the joint; the common fibular nerve winds round the fibular neck under the skin, where it is easily bruised, causing foot drop. Joint pain is carried by branches of the femoral, obturator, tibial and common fibular nerves, so hip disease can refer pain to the knee.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Osteoarthritis wears away the cartilage, most often in the medial compartment, causing pain, stiffness and bowing; X-rays show joint-space narrowing and a knee replacement resurfaces the worn ends. Ligament and meniscal injuries are diagnosed by examination and MRI. A hot swollen knee may be gout, pseudogout or infection, and a needle aspiration of the fluid tells them apart.

spine.title: Spine Anatomy
spine.intro: The vertebral column is a stack of 33 vertebrae, 24 of them movable, separated by shock-absorbing discs and bound by ligaments and muscles. It carries the weight of the head and trunk, allows the trunk to bend and twist, and shelters the spinal cord and the nerve roots that leave it at every level.

keyFacts.label: Vertebrae
keyFacts.value: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, 4 fused coccygeal

keyFacts.label: Curves
keyFacts.value: Cervical and lumbar lordosis, thoracic and sacral kyphosis

keyFacts.label: Discs
keyFacts.value: 23 intervertebral discs, about a quarter of the column's height

keyFacts.label: Spinal cord
keyFacts.value: Ends at about L1-L2 in adults; nerve roots continue as the cauda equina

keyFacts.label: Nerves
keyFacts.value: 31 pairs of spinal nerves leaving through the intervertebral foramina

keyFacts.label: Movement
keyFacts.value: Most flexion and extension in the cervical and lumbar spine; rotation mainly thoracic

sections.heading: A typical vertebra
sections.body: Each movable vertebra has a weight-bearing body in front and a bony arch behind that encloses the vertebral foramen; stacked, these foramina form the vertebral canal for the spinal cord. The arch carries a spinous process (the bump felt under the skin), two transverse processes and four articular facets that form small synovial joints with the vertebrae above and below. The facet joints guide movement and can wear like any other joint.

sections.heading: Regions
sections.body: The cervical vertebrae are small, with holes in their transverse processes for the vertebral arteries; the atlas (C1) supports the skull and nods on it, the axis (C2) provides the peg on which the head turns. Thoracic vertebrae have facets for the ribs and long sloping spines, so the thoracic spine is stiff. Lumbar vertebrae are massive to carry the body's weight and allow bending. The sacrum wedges between the hip bones to transmit weight to the legs, and the coccyx is the vestigial tail.

sections.heading: Intervertebral discs
sections.body: Between the bodies sit discs made of a tough ring of fibrocartilage (annulus fibrosus) around a gel-like nucleus pulposus. They absorb shock, spread load and permit small movements that add up to considerable flexibility. With age the nucleus dries and the annulus cracks; a herniated disc pushes nucleus material backwards into a nerve root, most often at L4-L5 or L5-S1, causing sciatica.

sections.heading: Ligaments and muscles
sections.body: The anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments run the length of the bodies; the ligamentum flavum joins the arches; supraspinous and interspinous ligaments link the spines. Deep muscles (erector spinae, multifidus) extend and stabilise the spine; the abdominal muscles and psoas flex it. Most back pain arises from these muscles, ligaments and facet joints rather than the discs.

sections.heading: Spinal cord and nerves
sections.body: The spinal cord runs from the medulla to about the first lumbar vertebra, wrapped in the same three meninges as the brain and bathed in cerebrospinal fluid, which is why a lumbar puncture below L2 can sample the fluid safely. Thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves leave through the intervertebral foramina; each carries motor fibres to a group of muscles and sensation from a strip of skin (a dermatome). Below the cord the roots hang as the cauda equina; compression there is a surgical emergency.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: Segmental arteries from the vertebral, intercostal and lumbar arteries supply the vertebrae and send radicular branches to the cord, which also has a single anterior and two posterior spinal arteries along its length. One large radicular artery in the lower thoracic region (the artery of Adamkiewicz) supplies most of the lower cord, and its injury during aortic surgery can cause paralysis.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Mechanical back pain, disc herniation, spinal stenosis, osteoporotic vertebral fractures and spondylolisthesis are the common spinal problems. Red flags such as leg weakness, numbness in the saddle area or loss of bladder control point to cord or cauda equina compression and need an urgent MRI. Injuries are assessed by the level of the vertebra and the spinal segment affected.

large-intestine.title: Large Intestine Anatomy
large-intestine.intro: The large intestine is the last 1.5 metres of the gut: the caecum with its appendix, the ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, the rectum and the anal canal. It absorbs water and salts from the liquid residue arriving from the small intestine, hosts trillions of bacteria, and stores and expels the stool.

keyFacts.label: Length
keyFacts.value: About 1.5 m, 6-7 cm wide at the caecum narrowing to 2.5 cm at the sigmoid

keyFacts.label: Parts
keyFacts.value: Caecum and appendix, ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, anal canal

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Superior mesenteric artery to the caecum, ascending and most of the transverse colon; inferior mesenteric artery to the rest

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Vagus as far as the transverse colon, pelvic parasympathetic nerves beyond; sympathetic fibres from the mesenteric plexuses

keyFacts.label: Transit time
keyFacts.value: About 12-48 hours

keyFacts.label: Water absorbed
keyFacts.value: About 1-1.5 L a day, leaving 100-200 g of stool

sections.heading: Caecum and appendix
sections.body: The ileum opens into the caecum in the right lower abdomen through the ileocaecal valve, which stops contents flowing backwards. The appendix, a blind tube 5-10 cm long, hangs from the caecum; its position varies, most often behind the caecum, which is why appendicitis can present in unusual ways. Its wall is rich in lymphoid tissue.

sections.heading: Colon
sections.body: The ascending colon runs up the right side to the hepatic flexure under the liver, the transverse colon hangs across the abdomen on its own mesentery to the splenic flexure, and the descending colon runs down the left side to become the S-shaped sigmoid colon in the pelvis. The colon's outer muscle is gathered into three bands (taeniae coli) that pucker it into pouches (haustra) and carry fatty tags (appendices epiploicae). The lining has no villi; it is a smooth mucosa packed with mucus-secreting glands.

sections.heading: Rectum and anal canal
sections.body: The rectum follows the curve of the sacrum, storing stool until defecation, and passes through the pelvic floor into the anal canal, closed by an involuntary internal sphincter of smooth muscle and a voluntary external sphincter of skeletal muscle. Stretch of the rectum triggers the urge to defecate; the sphincters and the puborectalis muscle allow it to be deferred.

sections.heading: Blood supply
sections.body: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the caecum, ascending colon and two-thirds of the transverse colon through the ileocolic, right colic and middle colic arteries; the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the rest through the left colic, sigmoid and superior rectal arteries. The marginal artery runs along the whole colon linking the two systems. The splenic flexure, at the junction of the two supplies, is the part most vulnerable when blood flow falls.

sections.heading: Venous drainage
sections.body: Veins mirror the arteries and drain into the portal vein, so colonic cancers spread first to the liver. The lower rectum and anal canal drain into systemic veins as well, so cancers there can spread to the lungs, and the connection between the two systems forms haemorrhoids when pressure rises.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Parasympathetic fibres (vagus for the proximal colon, pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2-S4 for the descending colon and rectum) drive peristalsis and secretion; sympathetic fibres slow the gut and carry pain. Because pain from the gut is referred to the midline, appendicitis begins as vague pain around the navel and only moves to the right lower abdomen when the inflamed appendix touches the parietal peritoneum.

sections.heading: Function
sections.body: The colon absorbs water and sodium, converting about 1.5 litres of liquid chyme into formed stool. Its bacteria ferment undigested fibre into short-chain fatty acids that feed the lining, make vitamin K and some B vitamins, and shape the immune system. Mass movements a few times a day propel contents into the rectum.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Bowel cancer, most often in the rectum and sigmoid, arises from polyps that a colonoscopy can remove; screening uses a stool test for hidden blood. Ulcerative colitis inflames the rectum and colon, Crohn's disease any part of the gut. Diverticula form in the sigmoid where pressure is highest. Appendicitis is the commonest surgical emergency.

breasts.title: Breast Anatomy
breasts.intro: The breasts are paired modified sweat glands on the front of the chest wall, lying over the pectoralis major muscles and made of milk-producing lobes embedded in fat and tethered by fibrous ligaments. They grow under oestrogen and progesterone, make milk under prolactin and release it under oxytocin, and they are the site of the commonest cancer in women. The 3D model shows each breast from the NIH Human Reference Atlas on the reference chest wall: the body of the breast, the lobes of the mammary gland, the lactiferous ducts and sinuses, the suspensory ligaments, the areola with its tubercles and the nipple.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: On the front of the chest from the 2nd to the 6th rib and from the edge of the sternum to the mid-axillary line, with the axillary tail extending into the armpit

keyFacts.label: Glandular tissue
keyFacts.value: 15 to 20 lobes of branching tubulo-alveolar glands, each draining through a lactiferous duct that widens into a sinus before opening on the nipple

keyFacts.label: Support
keyFacts.value: Fat, and the suspensory ligaments (of Cooper) that run from the skin through the gland to the deep fascia over pectoralis major

keyFacts.label: Blood supply
keyFacts.value: Perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery, the lateral thoracic artery from the axillary artery, and perforating branches of the intercostal arteries

keyFacts.label: Lymph drainage
keyFacts.value: About three-quarters to the axillary nodes, most of the rest to the parasternal (internal mammary) nodes along the internal thoracic vessels

keyFacts.label: Nerve supply
keyFacts.value: Anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th to 6th intercostal nerves; the nipple lies in the T4 dermatome

keyFacts.label: Hormonal control
keyFacts.value: Oestrogen grows the ducts and fat, progesterone the lobules; prolactin drives milk production and oxytocin milk ejection

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: Each breast lies in the superficial fascia of the front of the chest wall, extending from about the second to the sixth rib and from the lateral edge of the sternum to the mid-axillary line. A tongue of glandular tissue, the axillary tail, runs from the upper outer quadrant along the lower border of pectoralis major towards the armpit, which is why breast tissue and breast lumps can be found in the axilla. About two-thirds of the base rests on the fascia over pectoralis major and the rest on serratus anterior. Between the gland and the pectoral fascia lies the retromammary space, a layer of loose connective tissue that lets the breast move freely over the muscle; a cancer that grows through it fixes the breast to the chest wall. The nipple usually sits at the fourth intercostal space, though its position varies with breast size and age.

sections.heading: Structure: lobes, ducts and the nipple
sections.body: The gland consists of 15 to 20 lobes arranged like the spokes of a wheel around the nipple, each a tubulo-alveolar gland whose lobules of secretory alveoli drain into progressively larger ducts. Every lobe empties through a single lactiferous duct that widens into a lactiferous sinus beneath the areola and then narrows to open on the tip of the nipple. Smooth muscle in the nipple makes it erect with cold, touch or suckling, and the pigmented areola carries the small bumps of the areolar (Montgomery) glands, whose oily secretion protects the skin during breastfeeding. The lobes are embedded in fat, which gives the breast most of its size and shape, and the gland is tethered by the suspensory ligaments of Cooper, fibrous bands running from the skin to the deep fascia. A tumour that shortens these ligaments draws in the skin above it, the dimpling that warns of cancer.

sections.heading: Blood supply and lymph
sections.body: Blood reaches the breast from several directions: perforating branches of the internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery pierce the upper intercostal spaces beside the sternum to supply the medial part, the lateral thoracic artery from the axillary artery supplies the upper and lateral parts, and perforating branches of the posterior intercostal arteries arrive from behind. Veins drain mainly to the axillary and internal thoracic veins. Lymph drainage matters most clinically, because breast cancer spreads along it. About three-quarters of the lymph, especially from the lateral quadrants, passes to the axillary nodes, which surgeons group into three levels around pectoralis minor. Most of the rest drains to the parasternal (internal mammary) nodes along the internal thoracic vessels. Injecting a tracer beside a tumour identifies the first, or sentinel, node it drains to, which can be examined instead of clearing the whole axilla.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Sensation from the skin of the breast is carried by the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the fourth, fifth and sixth intercostal nerves, with the supraclavicular nerves supplying the skin of the upper part. The nipple and areola lie in the fourth thoracic dermatome and are supplied chiefly by the lateral cutaneous branch of the fourth intercostal nerve, so nipple sensation can be reduced or lost if that branch is divided during breast surgery. These nerves also carry sympathetic fibres to the blood vessels and to the smooth muscle of the nipple; the gland itself has no motor supply, because milk secretion is controlled by hormones. Suckling stimulates sensory endings in the nipple and the signal travels to the hypothalamus, releasing prolactin and oxytocin. Surgery in the axilla can injure the intercostobrachial nerve, leaving numbness on the inner side of the upper arm.

sections.heading: Function and hormonal control
sections.body: The purpose of the breast is lactation. During pregnancy, oestrogen, progesterone and placental hormones make the ducts branch and the alveoli multiply, and prolactin from the anterior pituitary rises steadily, but the high sex hormone levels block its action so that little milk is made before birth. Once the placenta is delivered, oestrogen and progesterone fall sharply and prolactin switches on full milk secretion within a few days; the first milk is colostrum, thick and rich in protein and antibodies. Suckling keeps the system going: input from the nipple sustains prolactin release and triggers oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli and squeezes milk into the ducts, the let-down reflex. Supply follows demand, and the high prolactin of frequent breastfeeding often delays the return of ovulation and periods, though ovulation can return before the first period, so breastfeeding only prevents pregnancy reliably under the strict conditions of the lactational amenorrhoea method: fully breastfeeding, no periods yet returned and the baby under six months.

sections.heading: Changes across life
sections.body: Before puberty, and in men throughout life, the breast is a small system of rudimentary ducts beneath the nipple that hormonal change or some medicines can enlarge (gynaecomastia). At puberty oestrogen grows the ducts and lays down fat, and progesterone develops the lobules once cycles become ovulatory; the lobules swell before each period, causing fullness and tenderness. Pregnancy enlarges the breast, and after the menopause glandular tissue gives way to fat. In trans women, breast growth usually begins about three to six months after starting oestrogen and continues over about two to three years, usually to a smaller size than in cisgender women. Trans women and non-binary people who have taken feminising hormones for several years are eligible for breast screening: those registered as female with a GP are invited in the same way as anyone else on the register, while those registered as male are not invited automatically and can ask their GP or local screening service to arrange it. Trans men who have not had chest surgery are eligible on the same basis and may also need to ask.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Breast cancer is the commonest cancer in women worldwide. It usually starts in the cells lining the ducts or lobules and can spread along the lymphatics to the axillary nodes, so a new lump, dimpled skin, a newly inverted nipple, blood-stained discharge or a lump in the armpit should be assessed promptly; a breast clinic combines examination, imaging and a needle biopsy. In England the NHS breast screening programme invites women, and anyone else registered female with a GP who has breast tissue, from the age of 50 up to their 71st birthday for mammography every three years. Most lumps are benign: fibroadenomas, cysts and fibrocystic change. A blocked duct during breastfeeding can lead to mastitis and, untreated, to an abscess. Breast cancer also occurs in men, though rarely. Chest masculinisation removes most but not all of the breast tissue, so a new lump still needs assessment, and augmentation implants sit over or under pectoralis major.

neophallus.title: Neophallus Anatomy
neophallus.intro: A neophallus is a penis constructed by surgery, most often as gender-affirming surgery for trans men and some non-binary people, and also after loss of the penis through injury or cancer. Phalloplasty builds the phallus from a flap of skin, fat and fascia taken with its own vessels and nerves, usually from the forearm or thigh, while metoidioplasty releases the clitoris enlarged by testosterone to stand free as a small phallus. Neither has erectile tissue beyond that of the clitoris, so structure, sensation and function depend on the tissue used and the stages completed. The 3D model, the Phalloplasty layer of the atlas, is schematic: a phalloplasty phallus with its glans, a lengthened urethra and a scrotum with testicular implants, drawn to typical dimensions on the reference pelvis.

keyFacts.label: Retained organs
keyFacts.value: In people assigned female at birth there is no prostate; the cervix, uterus and ovaries remain unless removed and still need care

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The neophallus is attached to the pubic region where the clitoris and labia were, its base over the pubic symphysis between the hip bones and above the urethral opening. In phalloplasty the clitoris is usually stripped of its surface skin and buried at the base of the new shaft, and the labia majora are joined below to form a scrotum. If the urethra is lengthened, the new urethra runs from the original meatus through a lengthened perineal segment and along the underside of the shaft to the tip; the vagina is usually removed, because a lengthened urethra beside a retained vagina is prone to fistula. Behind lie the perineal body, external anal sphincter and rectum. The urethra passes through the urogenital hiatus of the levator ani, between the pubococcygeus of each side, and then through the deep perineal pouch, where the external urethral sphincter surrounds it, and on through the perineal membrane; the puborectalis sling lies behind, around the anorectal junction.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: A phalloplasty shaft is a rolled flap: an outer tube of skin over fat and deep fascia, and a glans shaped later by a ridge and skin graft (glansplasty). The radial forearm free flap is a rectangle of skin taken with the radial artery, the cephalic vein and the lateral and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerves; a narrower strip of the same flap is rolled skin-inward to form the urethra. The anterolateral thigh flap, raised on the descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery, is thicker, usually stays on its pedicle and often needs a separate urethral lining. A metoidioplasty phallus is the clitoris itself, released from its suspensory ligament and the labia minora, with a urethra optionally built along its underside from labial and vaginal mucosa. Scrotoplasty from the labia majora with testicular implants completes either operation.

sections.heading: Blood supply and lymph
sections.body: A free flap lives only through its vascular pedicle. In radial forearm phalloplasty the radial artery is joined under the microscope to a recipient vessel in the groin, usually the deep inferior epigastric artery or a branch of the femoral artery, and the cephalic and accompanying veins to the great saphenous or femoral veins; the joins are watched closely for the first days, since thrombosis threatens the whole phallus. The hand keeps its supply through the ulnar artery and the palmar arches, confirmed before surgery. A pedicled anterolateral thigh flap keeps its own artery and vein from the lateral circumflex femoral system, so no microsurgery is needed. A metoidioplasty phallus keeps the clitoral branches of the internal pudendal vessels, so its erectile tissue still engorges. Lymph from the shaft skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

sections.heading: Innervation
sections.body: Protective sensation comes from the flap's own cutaneous nerves, the antebrachial cutaneous nerves of the forearm or the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, which are joined at the base of the phallus to the ilioinguinal nerve and to one of the dorsal clitoral nerves. Erotic sensation comes from the clitoris, whose dorsal nerves are branches of the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) and are preserved when it is buried at the base of the shaft. Regrowth is slow: the shaft is numb at first, sensation returns from base towards tip over months to a year or more, and the tip may never be as sensitive as the base. In metoidioplasty the clitoral nerves are preserved, so erotic sensation is usually retained from the outset. The forearm donor site is left with altered sensation.

sections.heading: Function and hormonal influence
sections.body: The aims are standing urination, sexual function and a body that matches the person's gender. A phalloplasty shaft has no erectile tissue, so it cannot become erect on its own; rigidity for penetration comes from an erectile device, inflatable or malleable, placed at a later stage once protective sensation has returned so the skin can guard against pressure damage. Orgasm comes from the buried clitoris and the reinnervated shaft. A metoidioplasty phallus keeps the natural erection and full sensation of clitoral tissue but is small, so penetrative sex is usually not possible; it allows standing urination if the urethra is lengthened. Testosterone maintains libido, clitoral size and the oiliness and hair of the skin; the shaft skin behaves as forearm or thigh skin, growing hair unless removed beforehand, and does not engorge with arousal.

sections.heading: Changes through the stages and over life
sections.body: Phalloplasty and metoidioplasty are options in gender-affirming care that some, not all, trans men and non-binary people choose; gender incongruence is not a mental illness, and the World Health Organization classifies it under conditions related to sexual health. A neophallus is built in stages over a year or more. Before surgery testosterone has usually enlarged the clitoris, and hair is removed from the donor skin that will line the urethra; hysterectomy and oophorectomy often precede the first stage, and vaginectomy is done when the urethra is lengthened. Later stages add glansplasty, scrotoplasty with testicular implants and, after sensation returns, an erectile implant. Swelling settles over months and the forearm scar matures over a year. The shaft is skin and fat, so unlike the clitoris it does not enlarge or shrink with hormone levels, although its skin ages and grows hair as forearm or thigh skin does, and implants have a finite life.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance
sections.body: Urethral complications are the commonest problems after phalloplasty with urethral lengthening: a fistula, with urine leaking from the perineal or shaft urethra, and a stricture, with scar narrowing the channel and slowing the stream, which may need dilatation, urethrotomy or graft repair. Flap loss from thrombosis is rare but serious and needs an urgent return to theatre. Erectile implants can become infected or erode through the skin, since there is no corporal tissue to anchor them. The forearm donor site is covered with a skin graft that can heal slowly or fail in part, and leaves a visible scar and altered sensation; hand function is usually preserved but the arm is splinted at first. Urinary infections and retention can follow the urethral stages. Screening follows the anatomy present: a retained cervix still needs cervical screening, which has to be requested from the GP by anyone registered as male, because invitations are issued on the gender marker held by the practice; a retained uterus or ovaries still need gynaecological care, there is no prostate, and residual breast tissue after chest surgery still needs assessment if a lump appears. Anyone catheterising a neophallus should know which stages are complete, as the urethra may be tortuous.
